R. A. Lafferty

Sweeny, the Operas,
and the Wars

The Three Armageddons of Enniscorthy SweenyFive diagrams with passages from the novel.

Sweeny says he composed the Armageddon operas to carry the wars away from the world. The detective Flanagan reports that the music instead helps to create events. The novel also sets two histories side by side, one in which the wars happen and one in which they do not.

The Scapegoat Operas

Sweeny says he drove the catastrophes out in the operas “like laden goats,” so that they would not happen in the world (p. 205).

Download diagram as PNG

The narrator says the scapegoat tricks had opposite effects, since perverted cults grew up around the abominable happenings once Sweeny had made them known (pp. 205–206). Flanagan reports that the music creates events in the world and is more powerful than the words (p. 346). In a letter to Pope Kirol I, Sweeny calls his account a “pretense of artful sublimation” (p. 317). In his final speech he says he gave the people a choice between Bloody Opera and Bloody Armageddon, and they chose Bloody Armageddon (p. 372).

Two Histories

The opera presents a history in which Franz Ferdinand is assassinated in 1914. In the history where the opera is performed, he survived and is now emperor, and Sweeny warns him that the stage may change his past (p. 239).

Download diagram as PNG

The emperor is still alive when their conversation ends (p. 239). On a smaller scale, Skantling’s old photograph changes after Sweeny’s caricatures deform his face (pp. 261–262). Woodbine argues that a version of the present lived by even one person is authentic and may still become the only version (pp. 299–300). He also says that his General Law of Dualities does not apply to the split between the world where war is unknown and the world where war is known (p. 305).

From the novel

The Evidence for the Wars

General Dredgefellow reviews Army records, pensions, sworn memories, and his own wounds, and grants that “some of the evidence is very convincing” (p. 356). He still rejects the wars, because the people do not behave as they would if the wars had happened (p. 358).

Download diagram as PNG

Dredgefellow discusses both earlier wars; his wounds and the continuing payments belong to the second (pp. 354–358). He says the evidence cannot be argued against but that there are ways to bury it (p. 356). At the end the narrator states that Armageddon has arrived and that the people scarcely care (pp. 373–374).

From the novel

Further passages

Sweeny’s Part

The Marshals require Sweeny to keep composing, and Grogg and his allies try to stop him. Sweeny goes on composing and hides “hammers” in the work, tricks meant to keep the fictions he is assigned from becoming fact (p. 265).

Download diagram as PNG

Sweeny welcomes an orchestrator who says that “the destruction is all that matters,” and counts himself lucky to have him (pp. 251–252). He reports an analyst’s view that his own input to the war material was possibly larger than anyone else’s but might be no more than 5 percent of it (pp. 318–319). The narrator tries to settle the question with a poll on whether Sweeny caused the wars, and he calls the response irrational (p. 368).

From the novel

Further passages

The Last Year

In the extended 1983 violence spreads and war comes to America (pp. 370–372). Ultimate Armageddon arrives before 1984 is officially admitted and before the people burn Sweeny’s tree (p. 373).

Download diagram as PNG

The narrator says the End-of-the-World War could be neither avoided nor delayed, but that the time left before it could be divided and subdivided again and again (pp. 364–365). In his final speech Sweeny says he has made the Earth stand still in its orbit and delayed the arrival of the dreadful year (p. 372).
